origin_lemma.etymology: 9349 bhaginī f. 'sister' Mn., °nikā- f. Kathās. [J. Gonda AO xxi 23 supports derivation from bhaga-² 'vulva' (which, if it belongs to the 'crooked' or 'defective' word-groups of bhaṅgurá- or *vaṅka-², might with a variant *bagha- account for *baghinī- ~ bhaginī-). But EWA ii 460 sees in it more prob. the feminine of bhagín- as an expression of good wish — bhágaḥ kanī́nām of RV. i 163, 8 — to an unwed sister (note that in NIA. bhaginī- is usu. the younger sister). The transference of aspiration from the initial to the interior presents difficulty, unless as a conscious avoidance of similarity with bhaga-² 'vulva'. The argument in AO xxi 30 that no *baghinī- is attested and that therefore the transference could have occurred only at the stage bhaïṇī- is not conclusive that a form *baghinī- never in fact existed between the age of Aśoka and the first emergence of Pk. bahiṇī-. It is significant that in bhāginēya- no such transference occurred. The new bahiṇī- belonged to the Centre, the older bhaïṇī- remaining on the periphery in Dard., S., L., P., some WH. dialects, EA., Or., and Ko. — For distribution of svásr̥- and bhaginī- in NIA. see AO xxi 27. — bhagín-]

rows.gloss: string of small bells worn by bullocks
rows.etymology: 106. Pr. ẓugˈo ‘bell’, ẓugˈeig ‘bell; rushing or roaring of water’, ẓuṅulˈeig ‘small bell’ appear etymologically related with Kal. gạṅgạí ‘large bell (typically tied to the neck of a male goat or bull)’. We deal here obviously with ideophones for which *gruṅ-, *groṅ-, *graṅ- can be reconstructed — Nuristani Kt. gřaṅˈaři ‘bell’ — West Himalayish Bun. koroŋkoroŋ ‘a bell’ and Darma kɔloŋ ‘bell (a type)’, and also Bodo gugrá ‘bell (kind of, round, tied to the neck of a horse)’ is almost identical with below Santali. The forms are ultimately borrowings from Austro-Asiatic: — Sant. ghugra ‘morris bells, a band of small bells tied round the ankles when dancing’ and here perhaps also ghanar ghunur ‘tinkling, jingling (sound of small bells)’, Korku ghuruŋgula, guruŋgula ‘string of small bells worn by bullocks’ and koɽoŋ ‘round brass bell for cattle’ — Bahnar grɛŋ- nɛŋ ‘small bell’ and Cua graneŋ ∼ gareŋ ∼ reŋ ‘bell’, Halang gəgraʔ gəgri̤ːŋ ‘jingling of bells’ and griːŋ ‘the rings of a small bell’, Sre gruŋ ‘bell’, Ngeq krlooŋ ‘buffalo bell’, Khmu krlɛːŋ ‘metal bell around an animal’s neck’, Thavung kalɛŋ ‘a small cylindrically shape bell’, etc. Note: Derivation of the the Pr. and Kal. form < OIA *ghuṅghura- ‘bell’ (4477), for which Turner suggests borrowing from Dravidian which he supports by quot- ing Kan. gugguri ‘curl’, is unlikely. Here more or less (in)directly connected are also the following: H. ghanghan- ‘(bell) sound, jingle, clink’, OIA *ghanaghana- ‘tinkle, clang’ (4425) which is according to Turner and Mayrhofer onomatopoeic.
